1.q: הַ⁠דָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֣ה אֶֽל יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ מֵ⁠אֵ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה
1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [7:1](ta:07). This clause introduces a new event.
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

2.q: כֹּֽה אָמַ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר
2.note: The phrase **Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:5. This also occurs in verses 5, 12, and 18.

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the God whom the people of Israel worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom the people of Israel worship]
The word **yourself** is singular here because it refers to Jeremiah. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **you** refers to Jeremiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has spoken to you, Jeremiah]

3.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Here, Yahweh is telling Jeremiah why he should write on a scroll what Yahweh says. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. This also occurs in verses 10 and 18. Alternate translation: [listen carefully]
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:5.
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:32.
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 8, 10, 11, 17, and 21.
See how you translated this expression in 29:14.

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean that **my people Israel and Judah** are the ones who are being held captive. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [my people Israel and Judah from the ones who have taken them captive]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to freedom my captive people]

Jeremiah is using **says Yahweh** to affirm that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the earlier generations of Israelites were the immediate **fathers** of the people he is addressing. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to their ancestors who lived long ago]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel and Judah, and the pronoun **it** refers to the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and my people will possess that land]

4.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **And these are the words** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

5.note: See how you translated this phrase in 24:8.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **voice** that is characterized by **trembling**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a trembling voice]

The terms **trembling** and **dread** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [We hear the cries of great fear, terror ]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trembling**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those who tremble]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dread**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people who are terrified]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [one living peacefully]

6.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Alternate translation: [I would ask you to inquire and see]

Yahweh is using the question form to make his listeners recognize that what he describes next is as unnatural as a man giving birth. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [that a male cannot give birth!]

Yahweh is saying **every strong man** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [nearly every strong man]

Yahweh is using **his hands on his loins** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he is gripped by anguish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [gripped with anguish]

By **his loins**, Jeremiah means the lower body, the area between ribs and thighs that is affected by fear or anguish. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his abdomen] or [his belly]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a woman giving birth** is overwhelmed by pain, so are the strong men whom Yahweh describes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [overwhelmed with pain as is a woman in labor]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the fear that these men feel were a color, **paleness**, to which their faces have turned. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And every face shows great fear]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **paleness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [have become pale]

7.note: Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of dread and grief. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How dreadful]

Yahweh says **there is none like it** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [there will hardly ever be a day like it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And it is a time when Jacob will suffer greatly]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **time** that is characterized by **distress**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And it is a distressing time for Jacob]

Here, **Jacob** represents the descendants of Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And it is a time of distress for Israel]

The expression **he will be saved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh will save Israel from it]

8.note: Yahweh is indicating that this event will happen at the future time that he has just described. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [And then, at that time]

Jeremiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh of Armies** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

8.q: אֶשְׁבֹּ֤ר עֻלּ⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל צַוָּארֶ֔⁠ךָ וּ⁠מוֹסְרוֹתֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֲנַתֵּ֑ק
8.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the control that foreigners had over his people were **bonds** that tied them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will end the oppression that weighs you down, and I will free you from those who control you]

8.q: אֶשְׁבֹּ֤ר עֻלּ⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל צַוָּארֶ֔⁠ךָ וּ⁠מוֹסְרוֹתֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֲנַתֵּ֑ק
8.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I will completely free you from the yoke of slavery that he has placed on you]

8.q: אֶשְׁבֹּ֤ר עֻלּ⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל צַוָּארֶ֔⁠ךָ וּ⁠מוֹסְרוֹתֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֲנַתֵּ֑ק
8.note: The pronoun **his** refers to the king of Babylon, who has been oppressing the people of Israel, while the pronoun **your** refers to Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon from upon your neck, Jacob, and I will tear apart your bonds]
See how you translated this name in 19:11.

9.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel and Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Israel and Judah will serve]

Here, **David** represents a descendant of David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and a descendant of David, their king]

10.note: This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **dismayed**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and be confident and calm]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

Here, **behold me** is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to save you]

The pronoun **your** refers to the people of Israel, whom Yahweh also speaks of both as **their** and as **him** in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and your children]
See how you translated “seed” in 29:32 where it is used with the same meaning.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verse 16. Alternate translation: [those who captured the people of Israel]

10.q: וְ⁠אַתָּ֡ה אַל־תִּירָא֩ עַבְדִּ֨⁠י יַעֲקֹ֤ב נְאֻם־יְהֹוָה֙ וְ⁠אַל־תֵּחַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל
10.note: The clause **my servant Jacob, do not fear** and the clause ** do not be dismayed, Israel** mean basically the same thing (God changed Jacob’s name to Israel later in Jacob’s life). The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [The declaration of Yahweh, “You my servant Israel, must not fear]

11.q: כִּֽי־אִתְּ⁠ךָ֥ אֲנִ֛י נְאֻם־יְהוָ֖ה לְ⁠הֽוֹשִׁיעֶ֑⁠ךָ כִּי֩ אֶעֱשֶׂ֨ה כָלָ֜ה בְּ⁠כָֽל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֣ם אֲשֶׁ֧ר הֲפִצוֹתִ֣י⁠ךָ שָּׁ֗ם
11.note: The word translated twice as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before, God’s instruction “do not fear” in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Fear not, because I am with you”—the declaration of Yahweh—“to save you. Fear not, because I will make a complete end of all of the nations where I have scattered you]
Here, **to** marks **to save you** as the goal or purpose of **I am with you**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between what he will do to the nations and what he will do to his own people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For I am with you”—the declaration of Yahweh—“to save you. For I will make a complete end of all of the nations where I have scattered you. You, however, I will not make a complete end of. And I will discipline you according to justice, though acquitting, I will not acquit you.”]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **end**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will entirely ruin all of the nations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [justly]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **acquit** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [but I will by no means leave you unpunished]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **acquit**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [I will certainly punish you]

12.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:5.

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **your breaking** before the information about it being **Incurable**. Alternate translation: [Your breaking is incurable]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the harm that had come upon his people were a **breaking** of the body that no one could cure. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The harm done to you cannot be repaired]

Yahweh is using these possessive forms to mean the **breaking** and the **wound** that the people had suffered. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the breaking that you have suffered; grievous is the wound that you have received]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **breaking**, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verse 15. Alternate translation: [your hurt] or [your affliction]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the suffering of his people were a serious **wound** on their body. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your suffering is severe]

13.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if his people were a defendant in court for whom no one was **pleading** a **cause**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There is no one taking up your case] or [There is no one supporting you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the suffering of his people were a **wound** for which there were no **medicines**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nor is there any relief for your suffering; there is no recovery for you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **healing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [nothing can make you well]

14.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the nations that had been allied with his people were their **lovers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All of your friends have forgotten you]

The pronoun **they** refers to **your lovers**, the nations that had been allied with Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your former allies do not seek you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were **an enemy** of his own people and has attacked them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have punished you as severely as an enemy would attack you]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [I have wounded you severely, as though you were my enemy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **discipline**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with a cruel one punishing you]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the kind of **discipline** that **a cruel one** would apply. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the kind of discipline that a cruel person delivers]
See how you translated this phrase in 13:22. This also occurs in verses 14 and 15.

15.q: מַה תִּזְעַק֙ עַל שִׁבְרֵ֔⁠ךְ אָנ֖וּשׁ מַכְאֹבֵ֑⁠ךְ
15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to tell his people that it does no good for them to protest against the punishment that they have brought on themselves. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It does no good for you to cry out over your breaking, your pain that is incurable!] or [You should not cry out over your breaking, your incurable pain!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the disaster that had come upon his people were a **breaking** of their body. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in 10:19. Alternate translation: [your disaster]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the suffering of his people were **pain** from an injury that no one could cure. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your suffering that will not end]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pain**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your painful wound]

16.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because of all this]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the nations that destroyed his people were animals **devouring** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of the ones destroying you will be destroyed]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

The expression **will be devoured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [others will devour all of the ones devouring you]

Yahweh is saying **all of the ones devouring you** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [those who devour you, without exception,]

17.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the restoration that he would give his people were the **healing** of a wound. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will restore you, and I will deliver you from your calamities]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **healing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will make you well again]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his people were a person whom others had driven away and called an **outcast**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have said that no one wants you]

The pronoun **they** refers to the nations that watched Jerusalem be destroyed. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the other nations have called you an outcast]

Yahweh is speaking of **Zion** as if it were a living thing that others could seek out or ignore. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [That is Zion; no one pays attention to that city]

17.q: כִּ֤י & נִדָּחָה֙ קָ֣רְאוּ לָ֔⁠ךְ & צִיּ֣וֹן הִ֔יא דֹּרֵ֖שׁ אֵ֥ין לָֽ⁠הּ
17.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for they have called you an outcast, saying, ‘She is Zion; no one is seeking her]

18.note: **Behold me** is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to restore]
See how you translated the similar phrase in Jeremiah 29:14. Alternate translation: [making things go well again for]

Here, **the tents of Jacob** represents the homes of the descendants of Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the homes of Jacob’s descendants]

The terms **tents** and **dwelling places** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the homes of Jacob, and I will surely have compassion on them]

The expression **shall be built** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the people shall build the city on its mound]

In this verse, the words **city** and **palace** are singular in form, but they refers to the cities and palaces of the land of Judah as a group. The phrase **the palace** includes the king’s palace but probably also refers to all the fine and luxurious homes in Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “palace” and “city.” Alternate translation: [the cities…and the palaces]

19.note: Yahweh is speaking of **thanksgiving** as if it were a living thing that could go out from the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And thanksgiving will be heard from them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [songs that thank me]

The pronoun **them** refers to the descendants of Jacob. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the people of Jacob, and the voice of those laughing. And I will multiply those people, and they will not become few]

The phrase **the voice of those laughing** represents the sound made by people who are rejoicing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the sound of rejoicing]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the sound of those laughing will go out from them]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **few**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [they will become numerous]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **insignificant**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and I will make them significant]

20.note: The point of this comparison is that just as the descendants of Jacob were secure and numerous in **former times**, so will they be again. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And his descendants will be secure and numerous, just as they were long ago]

20.q: וְ⁠הָי֤וּ בָנָי⁠ו֙ כְּ⁠קֶ֔דֶם וַ⁠עֲדָת֖⁠וֹ לְ⁠פָנַ֣⁠י תִּכּ֑וֹן וּ⁠פָ֣קַדְתִּ֔י עַ֖ל כָּל־לֹחֲצָֽי⁠ו
20.note: The pronoun **his** refers to Jacob. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Jacob’s sons will be as in former times, and Jacob’s congregation will be established to my face, and I will punish all of Jacob’s oppressors]

The expression **will be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will establish his congregation before my face]
Here, **my face** represents my presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before me]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:14.

21.note: Yahweh is using these possessive forms to mean the leader and the ruler who would come from among the people descended from Jacob. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the majestic one of Jacob … and the ruler of Jacob … from Jacob’s midst]

21.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֨ה אַדִּיר֜⁠וֹ מִמֶּ֗⁠נּוּ וּ⁠מֹֽשְׁל⁠וֹ֙ מִ⁠קִּרְבּ֣⁠וֹ יֵצֵ֔א
21.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Their leader of Israel will be one of their own people]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [And he will draw near when I invite him to come to me] or [I will bring him near, and yes, he will approach me]

The pronouns **him** and **he** refer to the ruler whom Yahweh has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And I will bring this ruler near, and he will approach me]

21.q: מִ֨י הוּא זֶ֜ה עָרַ֧ב אֶת לִבּ֛⁠וֹ לָ⁠גֶ֥שֶׁת אֵלַ֖⁠י
21.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no one would dare to come near to him unless he invited that person. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one else would ever dare to risk his life to approach me.]

Yahweh is using **has pledged his heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “has risked his life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who would dare to risk his life]

22.q: וִ⁠הְיִ֥יתֶם לִ֖⁠י לְ⁠עָ֑ם וְ⁠אָ֣נֹכִ֔י אֶהְיֶ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֖ם לֵ⁠אלֹהִֽים
22.note: Yahweh assumes that readers will know that this expression was the formal way of stating that he and the people of Israel were bound to each other by covenant. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And by covenant, you will be my people, and I will be your God]

23.note: See how you translated this phrase in 23:19.
